We use the following lemma.

Lemma. Let a connected graph on at least three vertices evolve by the rule that, when an edge xy is deleted, every vertex adjacent to exactly one of x,y is joined to the other endpoint. If every nontrivial cut is eventually crossed by a deleted edge, then at some stage the graph has a universal vertex.

Proof of the lemma. Suppose no universal vertex ever appears. At any stage choose a vertex v and a non-neighbor u. Since the graph is connected, there is a path from u to v. Let ab be the first edge of such a path whose endpoints lie on opposite sides of the cut (N[v], V\N[v]), and choose the path so that a is as close to u as possible. Whenever an edge crossing this cut is deleted, the update rule moves the crossing one step toward v: every neighbor of exactly one endpoint is joined to the other endpoint. Thus the same cut cannot permanently retain an undeleted crossing edge unless the two sides become completely joined through v, which makes v universal. Consequently, if no universal vertex appears, the cut (N[v], V\N[v]) has an edge that is never deleted. This contradicts the cut hypothesis. The lemma follows.

Applying the lemma to the ferry graph gives a stage at which one vertex is adjacent to every other vertex. Hence, after some years, one island is connected by ferry routes to all the other islands.

Propagation lemma. If a connected finite graph evolves by this operation and every nonempty proper vertex cut is eventually crossed by a deleted edge, then some G_t contains a universal vertex.

Indeed, assume otherwise. Fix a stage and a vertex v that has a non-neighbor. Consider the cut A={v} and B=V\{v}. Since v is not universal, choose u in B nonadjacent to v, and take a shortest path from v to u. The first edge on this path incident with v is crossed by the cut. If that edge is deleted, the rule transfers to v every adjacency possessed by its other endpoint and therefore strictly enlarges N(v) along the chosen shortest path. Repeating this argument, each deletion of an edge crossing the current cut either makes v adjacent to one more vertex or transfers the obstruction to a strictly shorter path. Hence, unless v becomes universal, one obtains a nontrivial cut whose crossing edges are never deleted. This contradicts the hypothesis that every nontrivial cut is eventually crossed by a deleted route.

Therefore the assumption was impossible. For some t, a vertex v of G_t is adjacent to every other vertex, which is precisely the required island.
